# The working life of Iānus: from the myths to the modern trades
Every age hires the same gods; only the job titles change. **Iānus** never stopped working.

Ovid's Fasti gives him the one great scene: the poet asks the two-faced god why he looks both ways, and Iānus answers for himself — the only extended self-explanation any Roman god gets in verse.

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) — which maps every flagship temple to the industries its archetype demonstrably resonates with, each match argued and open to challenge — seats this temple in **3 industries**. This file reads those seats the way they were earned: through the myths.
## At a Glance

- **Temple:** Iānus
- **Pantheon:** Roman
- **Domain of influence:** Beginnings, Doors, Transitions
- **Pattern seats:** 3
- **Sectors touched:** Technology & Innovation · Culture & Entertainment · Commerce & Governance
- **Strongest seat:** Cybersecurity & Digital Protection
- **Series:** The Resonance Files, No. 115 of 271
## The Myth at Work

**Fasti 1.** Ovid asks Iānus why, alone among gods, he sees both behind and before.  The god replies: whatever you see — sky, sea, earth — all things are closed and opened by my hand; I preside over the gates of heaven with the gentle Seasons; I am called Chaos, for I was the ancient confusion out of which order came. — that is not just a story. It is a business model, four thousand years early.

**Ianus Geminus.** Numa, the peace-king, founded the rite: the gates of the Ianus in the Forum stand open while Rome is at war, closed in peace.  Livy records that since Numa's day they had been closed only twice — in 235 BCE, in the consulship of Titus Manlius Torquatus, and by Augustus, who boasted of closing them three times — and Nero closed them again after the Armenian settlement. — remember the shape of that act. You will see it again, wearing a logo.
## The Seats

Each of these is argued in the atlas with a weight and a why-line. What the atlas cannot fit in one line is the whole myth — so here is each seat with its story restored.

### Cybersecurity & Digital Protection

*Threat defense, authentication, and digital trust. (Sector: Technology & Innovation)*

*The gate and its keeper; access control’s oldest patron.* Swap the costume and the sentence is indistinguishable from the myth. That is what a resonance seat means.

### Timekeeping & Calendar Systems

*Watches, calendars, and time sciences. (Sector: Culture & Entertainment)*

*January keeps his name; the year’s door is his.* — the atlas stops there, out of discipline. The myth keeps going: the function Iānus performs in the stories is precisely the function this industry sells.

### Startups & Venture Creation

*Startups, incubators, and venture capital. (Sector: Commerce & Governance)*

The why-line says it in one breath: *The god of beginnings; every launch is his threshold.* That is not a resemblance; it is the same act, performed in a newer building.

Read the myth again after the seats and it stops sounding ancient: Ovid's Fasti gives him the one great scene: the poet asks the two-faced god why he looks both ways, and Iānus answers for himself — the only extended self-explanation any Roman god gets in verse. The age changed. The work did not.
